1:
Robertson works from the word outward: the reed is the growing cane of the Jordan brakes, the writer’s reed, and the measuring-rod of Ezekiel, which is the sense here. Gill gives the measures, six cubits by the Jewish reckoning and ten feet by the Greek and Roman, notes that one version calls it a golden reed, and makes the reed itself the Scripture, the rule by which doctrine, worship and discipline are all to be tried.

Three words of the verse are probably not in it. Barnes reports that and the angel stood is wanting in many manuscripts, is rejected by three editors he names and marked doubtful by a fourth, and appears to have been imported from Zechariah. Ellicott agrees it must go, and draws out what the omission leaves: we are not told who gave the reed, nor who speaks the command, the whole transaction being impersonal.

Which temple is measured turns on one Greek word. Ellicott distinguishes the term for the whole sacred enclosure with its courts and porticoes from the term for the house of God itself, and illustrates it from the Gospels, where Christ teaches the people in the one while Zacharias goes into the other; the second stands here, so the house and the altar are measured and the courts are not. Robertson agrees the word means a sanctuary on earth that is nevertheless not the building in Jerusalem, and suggests the spiritual temple. Clarke stands alone against them, taking it of the actual temple at Jerusalem, and turning that into a date: it is presumptive evidence that the building was still standing when the book was written.

What the measuring is for divides them further. Ellicott takes it as protection, the counterpart of the sealing in the earlier vision, a resolve to keep part of the enclosure from desecration; he finds the background in Ezekiel but prefers Zechariah, whose vision of the man with the measuring rod is followed by the two olive trees which this chapter presently identifies with the two witnesses. Barnes reads it as assessment rather than protection — an accurate estimate of the true church as distinguished from every other body of men, and of the altar as the church’s doctrine of sacrifice. Henry offers three designs at once, preservation, trial against the pattern shown in the mount, and reformation of what is redundant or deficient; and he adds that the worshippers are measured too, whether they take Christ for their altar and lay all their offerings there. Robertson declines to choose, remarking that modern scholars do not know how to interpret the passage at all, and setting one who took it for a scrap of Zealot writing from before the fall of Jerusalem against another who denied any literal sense and read the whole eschatologically.

The two Latin fathers read the reed as a book. Victorinus makes it the Apocalypse itself, and adds a tradition about the Gospel that followed: when Valentinus and Cerinthus and Ebion and others of the school of Satan were scattered through the world, the bishops of the neighbouring provinces assembled and compelled John himself to draw up his testimony. He then makes the measure of the temple a creed — to confess the Father Almighty, and the Son begotten of the Father before the beginning of the world and made man in soul and flesh — and says no one worships at the altar but he who confesses this. Bede takes the reed for the office of writing the Gospel, not a vain lustre but the rod of the kingdom, and explains the command to rise: not that John was seated, but that all hearts are roused by the word to measure their writings and actions by the divine rule, and so to find what progress each has made.
2:
Three of them agree that the English is too mild. Barnes says the verb carries the idea of force, and that John was not merely to omit the outer court but to do some positive act marking it off as no part of the true temple; Ellicott calls leave out far too weak, the seer being told to pass it over as though reckoned profane; Robertson renders it flatly cast without, and adds that this court is left to its fate.

Who the outer court stands for is the question, and the answers run in four directions. Barnes keeps it historical: it is the court of the Gentiles, and by Hebrew reckoning those who came no nearer than that were simply not counted among the worshippers of God. Robertson fills in the architecture, the middle wall of partition beyond which no Gentile could pass, and observes the irony that the outer court had been a house of prayer for the Gentiles and is now given over to them in quite another sense. Clarke and Wesley take the treading down literally: Clarke of the Romans and the approaching destruction of the temple and the end of the whole Levitical service, Wesley of Jerusalem trodden ever since by Romans, Persians, Saracens and Turks. Ellicott and Gill make it a picture of nominal Christianity, and Gill’s version is the sharper. He explicitly refuses to read the outer court of the church of Rome, since the Gentiles who receive it are the Papists; the court is a third party, carnal Protestants, the bulk of the reformed churches, who have the name but not the nature of living Christians. Ellicott says much the same of Christendom at large, that the spirit of the nations, though nominally Christian, will be the spirit of worldliness, and that the outer court of church life holds the ebbing and flowing mass who stand idle in the market-place and have no oil in their lamps.

Ellicott alone presses what the treading means. Our Lord had said Jerusalem should be trodden down of the Gentiles, and the seer catches the deeper significance: there is a treading worse than the conqueror’s, when the world-power in men tramples the pearls of grace like swine and turns on those who gave them. The shrine, he adds, will be safe; the church must nevertheless undergo this.

On the period they converge. Ellicott and Robertson both set out the three forms the same span takes through the book — forty-two months here and later, twelve hundred and sixty days twice, and a time and times and half a time — and both trace it to Daniel. Clarke says only that it must be a symbolical period. Wesley alone will not have it symbolic: the months are common months and the days common days, the severe treading is still future and will not begin until the seventh trumpet and the end of the troublous times, and the whole span is but a small part of a larger reckoning he has worked out elsewhere.

Two smaller notes. Robertson reports that one commentator holds only the heavenly city can be called holy here, on the strength of the Sodom and Egypt of a later verse, but thinks the language may be merely symbolical. Gill traces the outer court to the court of the Israelites, where the great crowd of worshippers stood, and notes that the prophet who measured the temple did measure that court, where this seer is forbidden to.
3:
Clarke gives up, and says so. The verse is extremely obscure, the conjectures of interpreters as unsatisfactory as they are endless; he quotes a Latin judgment that they build conjecture on conjecture and declines to rehearse their opinions, adding that those who wish to be amused or bewildered may consult ancients and moderns alike. Robertson reaches the same place by grammar: the article seems to point to two well-known figures, but there is no possible way to determine who they are, and all sorts of identifications have been attempted.

The others attempt them. Gill lists and rejects two — Enoch and Elias, which the ancient fathers held and which he says the Papists greedily catch at, and the two Testaments, whose name, number and office fit but which can hardly be clothed in sackcloth, killed, and raised — and settles on the ministers and churches that testified against antichrist, naming the churches of Piedmont as bidding fair for the character, since they were on the spot when antichrist arose, were never dependent on Rome, suffered great persecution and continue to this day. Henry canvasses Enoch and Elias and the two churches of believing Jews and Gentiles before preferring eminent faithful ministers who not only profess but preach in the worst of times. Wesley takes them for two select instruments and says the supposition that they are Moses and Elijah is without foundation.

Ellicott, instead of identifying them, asks why two. He notes the legal requirement of two witnesses and then traces the pairing through Scripture — Moses and Aaron, Elijah and Elisha, Joshua and Zerubbabel, the disciples sent out two by two, Paul with Barnabas and then with Silas — and adds the observation that makes the point worth keeping: beyond the mutual support two can give, a world-wide work needs two different characters together, the energy and the sympathy, the elucidator of doctrine and the messenger to the conscience, the apologist and the evangelist, the Son of Thunder and the Son of Consolation.

Two small corrections stand behind the paraphrase. Barnes and Ellicott both note that the word power is not in the Greek at all, which reads simply I will give; Barnes says some word like power, privilege or boldness must be supplied to complete the sense, and that the meaning is not that God would send these witnesses but that he would permit them to exercise their gift during the time named. Barnes also declines to hold the number to two persons, taking it rather as a mark that the number would be small. Ellicott presses the verb the other way, that prophesying must be allowed a far wider sense than predicting, since what follows describes wonders, mighty words and a life that is itself a testimony.

Cyril of Jerusalem is here on the period rather than the witnesses, and is careful about his authorities. He grants the fearful leave to flee, quoting the command to those in Judaea to take to the mountains, while bidding the stout-hearted stand, since he does not despair of the nerves of the Church; and he limits the tribulation, both by the promise that the days shall be shortened and by the term of three years and a half. That term he will not take from apocryphal books but from Daniel, quoting the time and times and half a time, and beginning to reckon a time as one year. Henry meanwhile turns the same number into a calculation, that a day stands for a year, so that if the beginning of the period could be fixed the end might be seen; and he explains the sackcloth as the habit of men deeply affected by the low estate of the churches, where Wesley calls it the dress of the deepest mourners and Robertson observes only that the dress suited the message.
4:
Everyone sends the reader to Zechariah and then parts company over how far the parallel runs. Barnes reconstructs the prophet’s vision in detail — the golden candlestick, the bowl, the seven lamps, and the two olive trees feeding it through golden pipes, so that the trees become emblematic of a constant supply of grace — but says the apostle does not use the emblem in the prophet’s sense. Robertson puts it more bluntly: in the prophet the lampstand is Israel and the olive trees are apparently Zerubbabel and Joshua, but here the seer makes his own use of the symbolism, and the trees and the candlesticks are identical. Clarke declines to decide at all, saying only that whether prophet and apostle mean the same thing by these emblems we do not know.

Ellicott takes the openness of the prophet’s answer as the point. The two anointed ones are usually supposed to be Zerubbabel and Joshua, though others think Zechariah and Haggai; but the angel’s reply is general, the vision age-long, and those two men cannot exhaust the fulness of a vision that represents an abiding truth — that the oil of gladness and strength rests on men who rely not on might or power but on God’s Spirit. Gill and Wesley keep the type but move it forward: Gill makes the ministers of the gospel sons of oil because of the grace in them, the gifts bestowed on them, and their freely imparting both to others; Wesley says they will transmit the unction of the Holy One to others as the two of Zechariah’s day did, and calls the standing before the Lord a waiting on God without the help of man.

The powers that follow are traced to two men by all of them. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all identify the fire from the mouth with Elijah calling down fire, the shut heaven with Elijah’s drought, and the water turned to blood and the plagues with Moses in Egypt; Robertson adds that the drought in Elijah’s time ran three years and a half, exactly the period named here. Barnes will not have the fire literal, making it the power of destroying enemies as if their words were burning coals; Clarke reduces it to a commission to denounce the judgments of God on those who obstruct their ministry. Barnes also explains the shut heaven from an ancient opinion that rain was kept in the clouds as in bottles, quoting Job on the bottles of heaven, and then loosens even that into a figure for calamity withheld.

Wesley alone turns the powers into an argument about identity. Smiting the earth with all plagues as often as they will, he observes, is not said of Moses, nor of Elijah, nor of any mere man besides; and he asks how it is possible to understand this otherwise than of two individual persons. Everyone else has been reading the witnesses corporately, so the question is pointed. He also locates the waters, taking them to be those in and near Jerusalem.

Two grammatical notes are worth keeping. Barnes and Robertson both press the verb rendered will: it is not the sign of the future but denotes purpose, if any man wills or desires to hurt them — and Robertson adds that it is impossible to hurt these two until they have done their work. Robertson also notes that the condition is repeated in a changed form the second time, as of something less likely to happen, and with inevitable death attached. Gill widens the hurt as far as it will go: any injury to their persons or properties, opposing their writings, blaspheming their doctrines or hindering their ministrations, by open enemies or secret ones.
7:
All of them notice that the beast cannot touch the witnesses until their work is done. Ellicott makes the most of it: only when their work is finished has the wild beast power over them, for to every man there are the symbolical twelve hours in which his life’s work must be achieved, and then, but not till then, cometh the night when none can work. Wesley says simply that till then they are invincible, and adds that the fire no longer proceeds from their mouth once the work is over. Gill divides the two things, holding that the open public testimony ends before the last war while the prophesying continues to the end of the beast’s reign — and that being dead they will prophesy still, their very death foretelling that the ruin of antichrist is at hand.

Who the beast is nobody will say. Clarke lays out three possibilities and refuses to choose between them: if the passage refers to the Jewish persecution of Christians, some Jewish power; if to the early centuries, one of the persecuting emperors; if to a later age, the papal power, with the Albigenses and Waldenses as the witnesses nearly extinguished by the persecutions raised against them — and he closes with the remark that whatever is intended, the earth has not yet covered their blood. Robertson says nothing less than antichrist will satisfy the picture, notes that some see Nero, and then quotes a judgment he evidently prefers, that the words cover in effect all the martyrdoms and massacres of history in which brute force has seemed to triumph over truth. Ellicott is content to say the beast-spirit stands in irreconcilable antagonism to the Christ-spirit, and defers the description.

The great city divides them sharply. Gill denies it can be Jerusalem, which was destroyed before the vision was given and is nowhere in this book called the great city, and makes it Rome and the whole jurisdiction of the Roman antichrist. Robertson takes the opposite view, that the closing clause about where their Lord was crucified makes it clearly Jerusalem, while admitting that everywhere else in the book the great city is Babylon. Clarke gives both readings and then says he must leave all these things to others. Wesley is not merely for Jerusalem but for a particular patch of it: the ground where the cross stood, which he notes was enclosed within the walls by Constantine, and on that very spot he expects the bodies to be exposed.

On the unburied corpses the comment is historical. Barnes explains why the image bites, that among the ancients nothing was more dishonourable than to leave a body unburied, and that the Jews held it a special indignity; Clarke turns it into an accusation, that in popish lands a Protestant is not suffered Christian burial or a grave in a churchyard. Robertson notes the Greek has no word for lie at all, only their corpse upon the broad way, and that the number wavers between singular and plural.

The three days and a half set the day-for-a-year rule against itself. Barnes allows it may be literal or, more in keeping with the style of the book, three years. Robertson observes that the days of gloating are exactly as many as the years of prophesying but denies any necessary correspondence, and passes on a description of the spectators as at once fiendish and childish. Wesley calculates instead: supposing the period to begin in an evening and to take in Friday, Saturday and Sunday, it would cover the weekly festival of Turk, Jew and Christian together, so that all of them, with the heathen besides, would have full leisure to gaze.
10:
The rejoicing is read as a familiar thing rather than a strange one. Barnes narrows the word earth to the land in question, gives a string of places where the Hebrew and Greek words mean no more than that, and then says the witnesses had been so great an annoyance to the governing powers that there would be general exultation when their testimony was silenced — a thing, he adds, so common in the world that the language is easy to apply. Robertson calls the phrase for those who dwell on the earth an apocalyptic formula for the non-Christian world, describes the jubilant jollification over the silencing of the two prophets, and remarks that such a sense of relief is perhaps not seldom felt today when a preacher of righteousness is removed. Clarke and Robertson both trace the sending of gifts to the Jewish feast where gifts were exchanged and portions given to the poor. Wesley compares the Philistines making merry over Samson, and says the gift-sending will be by Turks, Jews, heathens and false Christians alike.

The revival is grounded in two Old Testament passages. Robertson and Ellicott both hear the valley of dry bones, Robertson noting that the very phrase they stood upon their feet is taken from it, and Ellicott adding a nearer memory still, the three days of the Master’s death-sleep, with the promise that where he is his servant shall be. Ellicott then draws the general rule — that there is a resurrection power in even rejected truth, and that if it be of God men cannot overthrow it — and supplies a date to prove it: the orator of a council in Rome declared in 1514 that resistance to the papal rule was at an end and opposers existed no more, and within three years and a half Luther nailed up his theses.

One word is disputed at the ascension. Gill reports that one printed edition and two versions read I heard for they heard, though the copies generally have the plural; Barnes says the more approved reading is the plural; Ellicott finds the manuscript authority divided with the balance inclining that way; Robertson notes a little evidence for the singular, which is what the seer uses two dozen times elsewhere. Wesley prints the singular without argument and says the voice was designed for all to hear.

What the ascent means is where they separate. Barnes insists none of it need occur literally, the whole being manifestly symbol: the witnesses would triumph as if they ascended, their silenced testimony would be heard again, and their vindication would be public. Clarke compresses the whole thing into eight words, that they enjoyed a state of great peace and happiness. Ellicott takes the ascension as the token that they have a portion with their Lord, and marks the one difference from Elijah — that this is not done in comparative secret, since their enemies see the exaltation, so that the cause which seemed dead revives and those who laboured for it are recognised; persecution, as the poet has it, dragged them into fame and chased them up to heaven. Robertson makes the same contrast with the ascension of Christ, which was witnessed only by a few friends. Wesley notices who is watching: the enemies had taken no notice of the rising, though some had been convinced by it already.
13:
Wesley thinks the thirteenth verse settles what the great city is, and argues it like a proof. Babylon is to be wholly burned before the mystery of God is fulfilled, whereas this city is not burned at all: a tenth of it falls in an earthquake and the other nine parts are converted. He then does the arithmetic. Seven thousand slain being a tenth of the inhabitants, the city held seventy thousand, and the remaining sixty-three thousand were converted — such a conversion, he says, as we nowhere else read of, so that there will be a larger and holier church at Jerusalem than ever yet. He adds a point of style: God is called the Lord of the earth earlier, when he asserts his right over the earth by the witnesses, but the God of heaven here, when he declares his majesty from heaven by taking them up into it.

The others read the earthquake as figure. Barnes and Robertson both take it for political convulsion and revolution, Robertson citing the prophets and the Gospels for the usage; Clarke calls it violent commotions among the persecutors and revolutions of states. Barnes treats the tenth and the seven thousand as proportion rather than count, a considerable part of the persecuting power. Gill makes it a commotion in the civil affairs of the nations within the Roman jurisdiction, like the one when pagan Rome was near its ruin. Ellicott asks whether it is accidental that seven thousand is the number of those who had not bowed to Baal, and gives the verse its motto: rejected reformation avenges itself in revolution, and the city which might have been purified by the word is purged by the spirit of judgment.

On the fear that follows, three of them note that fear is not usually reckoned a good motive and here is allowed to be one. Ellicott says good is effected even through fear, and that these, unlike those who repented not earlier in the book, give glory to God. Robertson passes on the observation that a general movement toward Christianity induced by fear or despair is a prediction fulfilled more than once in church history. Clarke has the remnant receive the pure doctrines of the gospel and glorify God for their own conversion. Wesley simply writes, blessed terror.

At the fourteenth verse Barnes stops to survey the field and gives it up as unprofitable. He declines to enumerate the opinions that have been held, calling the attempt humiliating and discouraging, refers the reader to two collections, and reports the view of one recent expositor: that faithful Christian witnesses with miraculous powers bore testimony against the corrupt Jews in the last days of their commonwealth, and that the Jews by destroying them brought an awful doom on themselves. Clarke takes the same road, making the three woes the seditions among the Jews, the Roman siege, and the sack of the city and burning of the temple, in which nearly a million men lost their lives.

Wesley dates them instead. The second woe he ends about the year 847, when the power of the Saracens was so broken by Charles the Great that they never recovered it; the prelude of the third he finds in the Roman see enlarging its claims, and in the year 755, when the bishop of Rome became a secular prince by Pepin’s gift of the exarchate of Lombardy. Ellicott makes the structural point that governs everything: the angel had declared the end should not be delayed beyond the seventh trumpet, so whatever view of the book is adopted must be governed by the plain fact that the seventh trumpet brings us to the very end. Henry adds only that the sounding had been suspended while the seer was shown intervening matters of great moment.
15:
Gill uses the seventh trumpet to clear away three datings. It cannot be the times of Constantine, since the turn of affairs then came under the sixth seal before any trumpet sounded; it does not belong to the German Reformation; and he names a writer who fixed the sounding at 1558, when the kings of Sweden and Denmark set up the gospel and Elizabeth came to the English throne. His own conclusion is that the angel has not yet sounded at all, so that nothing past can be meant. Barnes places it precisely where Gill will not: at the end of the twelve hundred and sixty years of the papacy, the point at which Daniel’s fourth kingdom is finished and the reign of the saints begins. Clarke reports the two schools without joining either, one referring it to the destruction of the Jewish state and the spread of the gospel among the Gentiles, the other to the millennium and the consummation of all things.

Ellicott corrects the English plural and makes it the point. It is the kingdom, not the kingdoms, of the world that has become Christ’s: the contest is not for the separate nationalities, whose political systems might continue as they are under his rule, but for the kingdom of the world as one thing — and he hears behind it the Psalm that promises the heathen for an inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth for a possession. Robertson makes the same observation dramatic. Satan was willing to hand over that kingdom on the mountain for a single act of worship; Christ scorned partnership with him and chose war instead, war to the hilt and to the end, and this, he says, is the crowning lesson of the book.

Wesley draws a structural argument from a contrast. At the opening of the seventh seal there was silence in heaven; at the sounding of the seventh trumpet there are great voices; and this alone, he says, is enough to show that the seals and the trumpets do not run parallel. He adds that the kingdom falls to God at once in heaven while several dreadful things are still to appear on earth.

At the elders Ellicott presses a translation. They are seated on thrones, not seats, the same word that is rendered throne of Christ and seat of Satan elsewhere; and he quotes an archbishop to the effect that the variation obliterates two great ideas running through the book, that the true servants of Christ are crowned with him and share his sovereignty, and that the antagonism of the prince of darkness develops as a parody of the heavenly kingdom. Robertson notes that the elders, though they have thrones of their own, fall on their faces in every act of worship, and takes them for the redeemed while the living creatures stand for the forces of nature. Clarke calls them the representatives of the universal Church.

The thanksgiving turns on tenses. Robertson observes that the perfect thou hast taken emphasises the permanence of the rule while the aorist that follows is ingressive, thou didst begin to reign. Clarke says the three tenses of the divine name together give the infinitude of God. Wesley notices the one that is missing: the usual formula adds who is to come, and that clause is here swallowed up, since he is actually come — so that thanking God for taking his great power is all one with thanking him that he is come. Barnes reads the name as the pledge that the God who has now established his church is unchanging; Ellicott hears the Second Psalm through the whole chorus, the raging of the heathen answered and their counsel come to nothing. Gill alone takes the whole address to be spoken to Christ.
18:
What the nations are angry at is answered differently. Barnes takes the anger for the whole long history of opposition, the persecutions and the slaying of the witnesses, seen in retrospect from the moment of triumph. Gill will not have that, since anathemas and massacres could hardly be matter of thanksgiving to the elders; he makes the anger a resentment at Christ’s power and reign, at the loss of the outer court, and at the loss of power, profit and plenty when Babylon falls. Robertson and Barnes both hear the Second Psalm behind it, and Robertson calls this the culmination of the world’s hostility.

The rewards are graded by two of them. Wesley reads the list as a descending scale — the prophets, the saints who were eminently holy, and then those who fear his name as the lowest class, adding that men who do not even fear God will have no reward from him — and insists that the reward comes of free grace and not of debt. Robertson notes it comes at the end of the day, at the Lord’s return, according to each man’s work, and observes that the small and the great stand in a case that does not agree with the rest of the sentence. Clarke reads the judging of the dead as avenging, the word being often so used, and takes the dead to be those slain for the testimony of Jesus. Wesley expands the last clause into a catalogue of how the earth is destroyed: by the rage of wicked men against all that is good, by wars and the desolation flowing from them, and by such laws and constitutions as hinder much good and occasion many calamities.

At the last verse Clarke stops and confesses. He has come, he says, to the part of the book deemed of greatest importance by the Protestant Church and yet peculiarly difficult and obscure; he has often acknowledged his own incapacity to illustrate these prophecies; he might have used the labours of others, but does not know who is right, or whether any writer on the book has hit the sense. He promises to insert another man’s exposition as the most probable he has seen, and leaves that author responsible for his own views. It is the fourth time in this chapter that he has declined the question.

Barnes uses the same verse to argue about where the chapter ends. The opening of the temple, he says, corresponds to the door opened in heaven at the start of the first series of visions, and therefore begins a new series rather than closing this one — which agrees with his earlier complaint that the chapter is improperly divided and should have closed a verse before. Wesley makes a different structural point: the lightnings, voices, thunders, earthquake and great hail recur in the same order when the seventh angel pours out his vial, so that one place answers the other, what the trumpet denounces in heaven being there executed by the vial on earth.

The ark divides the antiquarian from the devotional. Robertson and Wesley both note that the ark of Moses was gone, probably burnt when the first temple was destroyed, and Wesley concludes that this must be the heavenly ark of the everlasting covenant, of which the other was the shadow, shown now as a testimony that God will fulfil his promise to the uttermost. Ellicott returns to the distinction he drew at the first verse: it is the inner house that is opened, and opened to its innermost recess, as though the veil were rent anew, so that the children of God who are themselves his temple need be hidden no longer. Gill takes it as the restoration of pure worship and church order, with the ordinances purged of the corruptions introduced by Papists and retained by Protestants alike.
